title: Builders Runtime Thesis — Compact Positioning
summary: A compact internal brief framing Redwood as the runtime partner for engineering teams who need predictable latency, unit economics, and operational control for LLM features.
body:
Objective:
Create a short, actionable positioning nugget that the GTM and product teams can use when speaking with engineering-first buyers: platform engineers, ML infra leads, and product teams shipping live LLM features. This doc is intentionally opinionated and compact; use it as a seed for sales scripts, landing page headers, and internal briefings.

Problem framing:
- Teams have moved past model choice as the core product decision; the harder part is making models behave in production: consistent latency, predictable cost per interaction, and safe degradations under load.
- Existing options force trade-offs: lowest-cost inference often sacrifices SLAs, while turnkey APIs hide economics and routing choices.

Core thesis (one sentence):
Redwood is the runtime that turns LLMs into predictable product primitives — letting engineering teams trade the right units (latency, cost, reliability) on their terms.

Why that matters (pillars):
1) Predictable economics: deterministic tooling to measure and control tokens-per-feature (batching, cache, quantization recommendations) so teams can forecast cost against feature metrics.
2) Latency and reliability guardrails: routing and fallback policies, plus observability hooks, keep user-facing flows within SLOs even when models or regions degrade.
3) Operational ownership without building-model-ops: the platform gives config and rollout primitives (canaries, A/B, pinned versions) that map to product teams’ release processes.
4) Deployment flexibility: same API and control surface across hosted, reserved, and private installs — so teams don’t rewrite their stacks as requirements change.

Proof points (how we demonstrate it):
- Benchmarks: 99th percentile token latency comparisons for common prompt shapes (internal telemetry, anonymized).
- Cost playbook: real customer case study (anonymized) showing 30–45% unit-cost win via batching + KV cache + quantization.
- Reliability: documented fallback chain and recent incident postmortem showing graceful degradation.

Simple elevator pitches (choose one by audience):
- For platform engineers: “Redwood gives your teams a single runtime that enforces SLOs, exposes cost controls, and fits into your release cadence — no bespoke model-ops.”
- For product leads: “Ship LLM features with predictable latency and predictable bills — Redwood makes inference a product primitive, not a research bet.”

Anticipated objections and crisp rebuttals:
- “We can self-host and tune models ourselves.” → Rebuttal: Self-hosting treats every production problem as unique; Redwood codifies operational best-practices (routing, cache, rollouts) so you avoid repeated rework and get predictable economics faster.
- “Hosted vendors are cheaper and faster to start.” → Rebuttal: Short-term speed is real, but hidden per-unit costs and limited control create fragility at scale. Redwood’s hosted mode is optimized for predictable economics; Dedicated/Private options scale that predictability for enterprise needs.

Call-to-action and next artifacts to produce:
- Sales one-pager: two column layout (why it matters / proof points + quick customer story + CTA).
- Technical appendix: latency/cost microbenchmarks and production config examples (autoscale, cache rules, routing policy samples).
- Battlecards: competitor comparisons mapping to the four pillars above.

Open questions / TODOs (internal):
- Pull two anonymized customer cost breakdowns for the cost playbook.
- Finalize 99th pctl latency graphs for the common prompt templates.
- Draft one-sentence header options for marketing to test in experiments.

Notes to reviewers: keep feedback focused on the framing that resonates with engineers (operational levers, measurable economics) rather than model architecture. This should be developer-centric and action-oriented rather than research-y.
